title: What Photo Works Best for a Hit the Road Dude AI Video? A Python Pre-Upload Check for Format, Size, Blur and Exposure
summary:
"Which photo should I use?" is the question that decides most AI remakes of the Hit the Road Dude meme, also searched as the State Property meme. One photo goes in, and a 15-second clip comes out. In it, your face (or your dog's) sits at the open window of a white pickup, repeats "State?" and sends the visitor off. The model only knows what's in that one photo. A soft, dark or sideways upload shows up in the result.

I run hittheroaddude.app, one of the generators for this clip. This post covers the small script I use before uploading a photo anywhere. It checks the hard limits first, then flags the soft problems that usually lead to a weak result. It's plain Python with Pillow and NumPy, and I ran it on the synthetic test images below.

The hard rules vs the heuristics

Some rules are the site's, and some are mine. They're different kinds of thing, so the script keeps them apart.

Hard limits (from the driver photo guide, checked 2026-11-09):

  • JPEG, PNG or WebP
  • up to 10 MB
  • one clear photo of one adult or one pet, face visible

Heuristics (my own thresholds, not rules):

  • short side under 512 px: faces get mushy
  • low Laplacian variance: the photo is probably soft or motion-blurred
  • mean brightness far from the middle: too dark or washed out
  • lots of pure black or pure white pixels: detail is clipped
  • an EXIF orientation tag: the pixels are stored sideways, and some pipelines ignore the tag

The script can't check "one subject" or "face visible". Those need eyes, or a face detector, which this post skips on purpose. Pets break most face detectors anyway.

The checker 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Pre-upload check for a Hit the Road Dude driver photo.

Usage: python3 photo_check.py photo.jpg [more.jpg ...]
Needs: pip install pillow numpy
Hard limits come from the site (JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB).
Everything else is a heuristic warning, not a rule.
"""
import os, sys
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024          # "up to 10 MB"
ALLOWED = {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}      # "JPEG, PNG or WebP"
MIN_SHORT_SIDE = 512                   # heuristic: below this, faces get mushy
BLUR_MIN = 60.0                        # heuristic: Laplacian variance on 1024 px
DARK, BRIGHT = 60, 200                 # heuristic: mean luma range (0-255)
CLIP_MAX = 0.08                        # heuristic: >8% pure black/white pixels

def laplacian_var(gray):
    g = gray.astype(np.float32)
    lap = (g[1:-1, :-2] + g[1:-1, 2:] + g[:-2, 1:-1] + g[2:, 1:-1]
           - 4 * g[1:-1, 1:-1])
    return float(lap.var())

def check(path):
    errors, warnings, info = [], [], {}
    size = os.path.getsize(path)
    info["bytes"] = size
    if size > MAX_BYTES:
        errors.append(f"file is {size / 1048576:.1f} MB, limit is 10 MB")
    try:
        im = Image.open(path)
        fmt = im.format
    except Exception as e:
        return {"path": path, "errors": [f"not an image Pillow can read: {e}"],
                "warnings": [], "info": info}
    info["format"] = fmt
    if fmt not in ALLOWED:
        errors.append(f"format {fmt}; upload JPEG, PNG or WebP")
    orient = im.getexif().get(0x0112, 1)
    if orient not in (1, None):
        warnings.append(f"EXIF orientation {orient}: the raw pixels are rotated; "
                        "re-save upright if the preview looks sideways")
    im = ImageOps.exif_transpose(im)
    w, h = im.size
    info["size"] = f"{w}x{h}"
    if min(w, h) < MIN_SHORT_SIDE:
        warnings.append(f"short side {min(w, h)} px is small; use the original photo")
    if getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1:
        warnings.append("animated file: only one frame will matter")
    gray = im.convert("L")
    gray.thumbnail((1024, 1024))
    a = np.asarray(gray)
    sharp = laplacian_var(a)
    mean = float(a.mean())
    clipped = float(((a <= 3) | (a >= 252)).mean())
    info.update(sharpness=round(sharp, 1), mean_luma=round(mean, 1),
                clipped=round(clipped, 3))
    if sharp < BLUR_MIN:
        warnings.append(f"looks soft (sharpness {sharp:.0f} < {BLUR_MIN:.0f})")
    if mean < DARK:
        warnings.append(f"looks dark (mean {mean:.0f})")
    elif mean > BRIGHT:
        warnings.append(f"looks washed out (mean {mean:.0f})")
    if clipped > CLIP_MAX:
        warnings.append(f"{clipped:.0%} of pixels are pure black or white")
    return {"path": path, "errors": errors, "warnings": warnings, "info": info}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    worst = 0
    for p in sys.argv[1:]:
        r = check(p)
        status = "FAIL" if r["errors"] else ("WARN" if r["warnings"] else "OK")
        worst = max(worst, {"OK": 0, "WARN": 1, "FAIL": 2}[status])
        print(f"{status:4}  {os.path.basename(p)}  {r['info']}")
        for m in r["errors"]:
            print(f"      error: {m}")
        for m in r["warnings"]:
            print(f"      warn:  {m}")
    sys.exit(worst)

A few implementation notes:

  • ImageOps.exif_transpose before measuring. Phones often save a portrait shot as landscape pixels plus an "orientation = 6" tag. If you measure or crop before applying it, you're working on a sideways image.
  • Sharpness on a 1024 px thumbnail. Laplacian variance depends on resolution, so the image is downsized first. That keeps the threshold comparable between a 12 MP phone photo and a 1 MP screenshot.
  • The Laplacian is four NumPy slices. There's no OpenCV dependency. It's the classic 3×3 kernel (0 1 0 / 1 -4 1 / 0 1 0), written as shifted arrays.
  • Exit codes: 0 means everything passed, 1 means warnings only, and 2 means a hard limit failed. That makes it easy to use in a shell loop or a pre-commit-style script.

Test images

No real faces were used here. The generator script draws a head-shaped ellipse, shoulders and random line texture, then saves the variants that typically go wrong:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Make synthetic test photos (no real faces) for photo_check.py."""
import os
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFilter

os.makedirs("samples", exist_ok=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

def portrait(w=1200, h=1600):
    im = Image.new("RGB", (w, h), (120, 150, 170))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(im)
    d.ellipse((w*0.3, h*0.2, w*0.7, h*0.55), fill=(205, 170, 140))   # "head"
    d.rectangle((w*0.2, h*0.6, w*0.8, h), fill=(40, 60, 90))           # "shoulders"
    for _ in range(400):                                                # texture
        x, y = rng.integers(0, w), rng.integers(0, h)
        c = tuple(int(v) for v in rng.integers(0, 255, 3))
        d.line((x, y, x + rng.integers(-30, 30), y + rng.integers(-30, 30)), fill=c, width=2)
    return im

base = portrait()
base.save("samples/good.jpg", quality=90)
base.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(6)).save("samples/blurry.jpg", quality=90)
Image.eval(base, lambda v: v // 5).save("samples/dark.jpg", quality=90)
base.resize((300, 400)).save("samples/tiny.png")
base.save("samples/still.gif")
# sideways phone photo: pixels stored rotated, EXIF says "rotate 90 CW"
rot = base.rotate(90, expand=True)
exif = Image.Exif(); exif[0x0112] = 6
rot.save("samples/sideways.jpg", quality=90, exif=exif)
# oversized: 3000x4000 noise PNG is far above 10 MB
Image.fromarray(rng.integers(0, 255, (4000, 3000, 3), dtype=np.uint8)).save("samples/huge.png")
for f in sorted(os.listdir("samples")):
    print(f, os.path.getsize(f"samples/{f}"))

Output from python3 make_samples.py && python3 photo_check.py samples/* (lightly trimmed):

WARN  blurry.jpg   sharpness 0.5  -> looks soft (sharpness 1 < 60)
WARN  dark.jpg     sharpness 6.9, mean_luma 25.3 -> looks soft, looks dark (mean 25)
OK    good.jpg     1200x1600, sharpness 164.8, mean_luma 126.1
FAIL  huge.png     error: file is 34.4 MB, limit is 10 MB
WARN  sideways.jpg EXIF orientation 6: the raw pixels are rotated
FAIL  still.gif    error: format GIF; upload JPEG, PNG or WebP
WARN  tiny.png     short side 300 px is small; use the original photo

One result is worth explaining. The dark photo is also flagged as soft, even though it's the same drawing as good.jpg. Laplacian variance measures edge contrast, so darkening an image lowers it. Fix exposure first, then re-check sharpness. Otherwise you'll go hunting for a sharper photo you don't need.

Fixing what's fixable

Format, size and orientation can be fixed in code. Blur and bad light can't, so use a different photo for those. This helper bakes the rotation into the pixels, caps the long side at 2048 px and re-saves as JPEG:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Re-save a photo upright as a JPEG under 10 MB (long side <= 2048 px).

Usage: python3 fix_photo.py in.ext out.jpg
"""
import os, sys
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
im = ImageOps.exif_transpose(Image.open(src)).convert("RGB")  # bake in rotation
im.thumbnail((2048, 2048), Image.LANCZOS)                     # never upscales
for q in (92, 85, 78, 70):
    im.save(dst, "JPEG", quality=q, optimize=True)            # no EXIF copied
    if os.path.getsize(dst) <= 10 * 1024 * 1024:
        break
print(dst, im.size, os.path.getsize(dst), "bytes, quality", q)

I ran the fixer on the three failing files, then re-checked them:

samples/fixed-huge.jpg (1536, 2048) 2136089 bytes, quality 92
samples/fixed-sideways.jpg (1200, 1600) 92914 bytes, quality 92
samples/fixed-still.jpg (1200, 1600) 99131 bytes, quality 92
OK    fixed-huge.jpg ...
OK    fixed-sideways.jpg ...
OK    fixed-still.jpg ...

Side effect: Pillow doesn't copy EXIF unless you pass it, so the re-saved JPEG also drops GPS and camera metadata. For a photo you're about to upload to any web service, that's usually what you want.

What the numbers can't tell you

The checks above are necessary but not sufficient. Before uploading, also look at the photo yourself:

  1. One subject. In a group photo the generator may pick the wrong face. Crop down to one person or one pet.
  2. Face and shoulders, not a scene. A wide shot of you next to a truck is the output look, not a useful input. The guide puts it as: "A wide shot of a truck is what the result looks like, not a useful upload."
  3. Your right to use it. Use yourself, an adult who agreed, or your own pet. Don't use a photo just because it's online (acceptable use).
  4. Pets: eyes, nose and mouth visible, roughly facing the camera. The dog and cat guide has a table of photos that do and don't work.

Where the photo goes next

On my studio, the photo is the only creative input. There's no prompt box, and the scene and lines are saved in a preset. You pick 480p or 720p, see the total on the button and pay before anything is generated. The live pricing page on 2026-11-09 listed $9.99 at 480p (6 credits) or $12.99 at 720p (14 credits) per clip. Signed-in accounts can also buy one-time credit packs. There's no subscription and no free clip, so a 30-second photo check costs less than a wasted run.

If you're ready, the create page takes the file directly. If the result still looks off, the help page points out that "Most problems come from the photo." That's why this script exists.

title: Why does osFoundry make Claude name the exact Slides tab and key every citation?
summary:
This is the create call a Claude connection gets for osFoundry Notes, from an unauthenticated tools/list against the public MCP endpoint on 2026-11-09, trimmed:

{"name": "create_note_tab",
 "description": "Create a new Slides or Sheet tab in an approved Note. Use the version from list_note_tabs; returns the exact new tab ID for later edits. An optional outline fills a Slides tab. A repeated idempotency key returns the first tab.",
 "inputSchema": {
   "required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "tab_type"],
   "properties": {
     "tab_type": {"enum": ["slides", "sheet"]},
     "label": {"type": "string"},
     "slides": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1, "maxItems": 20,
                "items": {"required": ["title"], "additionalProperties": false,
                          "properties": {"title": {}, "body": {}, "notes": {}}}}},
   "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

Its two neighbours for this job:

{"name": "add_note_source",
 "description": "Add an HTTP or HTTPS citation to the Sources tab of an approved Note. Uses the Note version and an idempotency key; returns the new source ID.",
 "inputSchema": {"required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "title", "url"]}}

{"name": "list_note_tabs",
 "description": "List every tab instance and its type. A Note may have multiple Slides or Sheet tabs; use the exact tab ID returned here."}

Three phrases carry the design: "every tab instance", "returns the exact new tab ID", and "a repeated idempotency key returns the first". The rest of this post rebuilds the tools in Python and measures what each of those phrases prevents. Optimistic locking on the Note version is the subject of a separate post and only shows up here where it interacts with the other two.

What can Claude actually put on a slide?

Less than the desktop app's own assistant. Inside osFoundry, the Note assistant's slide_create_deck_from_outline and slide_add_slide (in apps/web/src/screens/notes/lib/note-surface-tools.ts) take layouts, bullets, two-column content, tables, images and one of five themes. The connector's outline item is title, body, notes, with additionalProperties: false. edit_note_tab offers slide_add for one slide and slides_add_outline for an array, both with the same three fields.

code/note_store.py loads the saved tools/list response and checks payloads against it with a tiny validator (required, enum, additionalProperties, minItems/maxItems). Eight payloads a model might plausibly send:

edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "body": "3 links"}  -> ok
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "index": 0}         -> unexpected index
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add", "slides": [{"title": "a"}]}            -> operation: not in enum

title: How to Control LLM API Costs: Token Budgets, Batching and a Budget Guard in Python
summary:
Most surprises on an LLM bill do not come from the price per token. They come from the call pattern: how many requests you send, how much context each one carries, and whether anything stops a loop that runs too long.

In this tutorial you will build a small budget guard in Python, learn how to count tokens before you send a request, and see why batching often matters more than choosing a cheaper model. The examples use a generic client, so you can adapt them to any provider.

Cost is driven by the call pattern

Provider pricing is simple: input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price. The bill is large when one of these grows without a limit:

  • Number of calls (a loop over thousands of items).
  • Input size per call (the full document sent each time).
  • Output size (no maximum set).
  • Retries (a failing call repeated automatically).

I learned this in a real project. A script called a paid data API once per keyword, 1,984 single requests in one day, and the day cost 23.92 USD. The same data was available through a batch endpoint that accepts up to 700 items per call. Batched, the cost would have been roughly 2 to 3 USD. The price per item never changed. Only the call pattern did.

LLM APIs behave the same way, so apply the same thinking before you write the loop.

Step 1: Count tokens before you send

You can estimate the cost of a request before you make it. Many providers publish a tokenizer or a token counting endpoint. If yours does not, a rough rule for English text is about four characters per token. It is an estimate, so keep a safety margin.

def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    # Rough estimate for English text. Replace with your provider's tokenizer.
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)

Use the real tokenizer when accuracy matters. Use the estimate when you only need to catch a request that is ten times bigger than expected.

Step 2: A budget guard class

The guard keeps a running total and refuses to continue when the budget is used up. It raises an exception, so a runaway loop stops instead of billing you all night.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


class BudgetExceeded(Exception):
    pass


@dataclass
class BudgetGuard:
    limit_usd: float
    input_price_per_1m: float
    output_price_per_1m: float
    spent_usd: float = field(default=0.0, init=False)

    def check(self, input_tokens: int, max_output_tokens: int) -> None:
        worst_case = self._cost(input_tokens, max_output_tokens)
        if self.spent_usd + worst_case > self.limit_usd:
            raise BudgetExceeded(
                f"Budget {self.limit_usd:.2f} USD would be exceeded "
                f"(spent {self.spent_usd:.2f}, next call up to {worst_case:.2f})"
            )

    def record(self, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> None:
        self.spent_usd += self._cost(input_tokens, output_tokens)

    def _cost(self, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> float:
        return (
            input_tokens * self.input_price_per_1m
            + output_tokens * self.output_price_per_1m
        ) / 1_000_000

The prices are constructor arguments on purpose. Prices change, and a constant buried in the code goes stale. Read them from your provider's current price list.

Use it around every call:

guard = BudgetGuard(limit_usd=5.0, input_price_per_1m=3.0, output_price_per_1m=15.0)

def ask(client, prompt: str) -> str:
    max_out = 500
    guard.check(estimate_tokens(prompt), max_out)
    response = client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=max_out)  # your provider call
    guard.record(response.input_tokens, response.output_tokens)
    return response.text

Two design choices are worth noting. The check uses the worst case (full max_tokens output), so the guard errs on the safe side. And the exception is loud: you want a stopped job and a log line, not a silent fallback.

Step 3: Batching, collect first and send once

The most common anti-pattern looks like this:

for item in items:                 # 2,000 items
    result = ask(client, f"Classify: {item}")

Each call repeats the same instructions, adds network overhead, and multiplies the chance of hitting a rate limit. When the task allows it, collect first and send once:

def chunks(seq, size):
    for i in range(0, len(seq), size):
        yield seq[i:i + size]

for batch in chunks(items, 50):
    numbered = "\n".join(f"{n}. {text}" for n, text in enumerate(batch, 1))
    prompt = (
        "Classify each numbered item as positive, neutral or negative. "
        "Answer with one line per item in the format ': '.\n\n"
        + numbered
    )
    answer = ask(client, prompt)

Now 2,000 items need 40 calls instead of 2,000, and the instructions are sent 40 times instead of 2,000 times. Test the batch size on a sample: very large batches can reduce answer quality, and a parsing step must handle a missing line.

Many providers also offer an asynchronous batch interface at a reduced price for jobs that can wait. If your job is not interactive, check for it.

Step 4: Avoid input bloat

The second big multiplier is context. If you send the entire document on every call and only one paragraph changed, you pay for the unchanged part again and again.

Practical rules:

  • Send only the part that the model needs for this question.
  • Keep the fixed instructions short, and remove examples that do not change the answer.
  • For chat-style flows, summarize old turns instead of replaying them in full.
  • If your provider supports prompt caching, put the stable part at the start of the prompt and the variable part at the end, then check the pricing rules for cached input.

Step 5: Monitoring and daily caps

A guard inside the script protects one job. You also need a limit across jobs:

  1. Set a hard monthly or daily spending limit in your provider's dashboard, if it offers one.
  2. Log every call with timestamp, job name, input tokens and output tokens. A CSV file is enough to start.
  3. Review the log once a week and look for the job whose call count jumped. 
import csv, time

def log_call(job: str, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int, path="llm_calls.csv"):
    with open(path, "a", newline="") as f:
        csv.writer(f).writerow([time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), job, input_tokens, output_tokens])

Call log_call right after guard.record. The first time a loop goes wrong, this file tells you which job caused it.

Most surprises on an LLM bill do not come from the price per token. They come from the call pattern: how many requests you send, how much context each one carries, and whether anything stops a loop that runs too long.

In this tutorial you will build a small budget guard in Python, learn how to count tokens before you send a request, and see why batching often matters more than choosing a cheaper model. The examples use a generic client, so you can adapt them to any provider.

Cost is driven by the call pattern

Provider pricing is simple: input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price. The bill is large when one of these grows without a limit:

  • Number of calls (a loop over thousands of items).
  • Input size per call (the full document sent each time).
  • Output size (no maximum set).
  • Retries (a failing call repeated automatically).

I learned this in a real project. A script called a paid data API once per keyword, 1,984 single requests in one day, and the day cost 23.92 USD. The same data was available through a batch endpoint that accepts up to 700 items per call. Batched, the cost would have been roughly 2 to 3 USD. The price per item never changed. Only the call pattern did.

LLM APIs behave the same way, so apply the same thinking before you write the loop.

Step 1: Count tokens before you send

You can estimate the cost of a request before you make it. Many providers publish a tokenizer or a token counting endpoint. If yours does not, a rough rule for English text is about four characters per token. It is an estimate, so keep a safety margin.

def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    # Rough estimate for English text. Replace with your provider's tokenizer.
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)

Use the real tokenizer when accuracy matters. Use the estimate when you only need to catch a request that is ten times bigger than expected.

Step 2: A budget guard class

The guard keeps a running total and refuses to continue when the budget is used up. It raises an exception, so a runaway loop stops instead of billing you all night.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


class BudgetExceeded(Exception):
    pass


@dataclass
class BudgetGuard:
    limit_usd: float
    input_price_per_1m: float
    output_price_per_1m: float
    spent_usd: float = field(default=0.0, init=False)

    def check(self, input_tokens: int, max_output_tokens: int) -> None:
        worst_case = self._cost(input_tokens, max_output_tokens)
        if self.spent_usd + worst_case > self.limit_usd:
            raise BudgetExceeded(
                f"Budget {self.limit_usd:.2f} USD would be exceeded "
                f"(spent {self.spent_usd:.2f}, next call up to {worst_case:.2f})"
            )

    def record(self, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> None:
        self.spent_usd += self._cost(input_tokens, output_tokens)

    def _cost(self, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> float:
        return (
            input_tokens * self.input_price_per_1m
            + output_tokens * self.output_price_per_1m
        ) / 1_000_000

The prices are constructor arguments on purpose. Prices change, and a constant buried in the code goes stale. Read them from your provider's current price list.

Use it around every call:

guard = BudgetGuard(limit_usd=5.0, input_price_per_1m=3.0, output_price_per_1m=15.0)

def ask(client, prompt: str) -> str:
    max_out = 500
    guard.check(estimate_tokens(prompt), max_out)
    response = client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=max_out)  # your provider call
    guard.record(response.input_tokens, response.output_tokens)
    return response.text

Two design choices are worth noting. The check uses the worst case (full max_tokens output), so the guard errs on the safe side. And the exception is loud: you want a stopped job and a log line, not a silent fallback.

The most common anti-pattern looks like this:

    result = ask(client, f"Classify: {item}")

def chunks(seq, size):
    for i in range(0, len(seq), size):
        yield seq[i:i + size]

for batch in chunks(items, 50):

        "Classify each numbered item as positive, neutral or negative. "
        "Answer with one line per item in the format ': '.\n\n"
        + numbered
    )
    answer = ask(client, prompt)

Now 2,000 items need 40 calls instead of 2,000, and the instructions are sent 40 times instead of 2,000 times. Test the batch size on a sample: very large batches can reduce answer quality, and a parsing step must handle a missing line.

Many providers also offer an asynchronous batch interface at a reduced price for jobs that can wait. If your job is not interactive, check for it.

Step 4: Avoid input bloat

The second big multiplier is context. If you send the entire document on every call and only one paragraph changed, you pay for the unchanged part again and again.

Practical rules:

  • Send only the part that the model needs for this question.
  • Keep the fixed instructions short, and remove examples that do not change the answer.
  • For chat-style flows, summarize old turns instead of replaying them in full.
  • If your provider supports prompt caching, put the stable part at the start of the prompt and the variable part at the end, then check the pricing rules for cached input.

Step 5: Monitoring and daily caps

A guard inside the script protects one job. You also need a limit across jobs:

  1. Set a hard monthly or daily spending limit in your provider's dashboard, if it offers one.
  2. Log every call with timestamp, job name, input tokens and output tokens. A CSV file is enough to start.
  3. Review the log once a week and look for the job whose call count jumped.

def log_call(job: str, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int, path="llm_calls.csv"):

title: Cómo etiquetar texto con un LLM local para que solo responda con tus etiquetas
summary:
Etiquetar filas con un modelo de lenguaje parece la tarea más fácil que se le puede dar. Envías cada fila con una instrucción del tipo "queja, elogio o pregunta, solo la etiqueta", guardas lo que vuelve y cuentas. La acción Run Model de la pantalla Datasets de la aplicación de escritorio osFoundry funciona así: BatchInferenceDialog.tsx envía cada fila por separado como la instrucción, una línea en blanco y el texto de la fila, y guarda la respuesta como una columna nueva. A continuación, ese bucle se reconstruye en Python con mlx-lm y se ejecuta sobre 312 reseñas de una tienda cuyas etiquetas correctas se conocen, para ver qué devuelve en realidad. Un modelo de 3B acertó casi todas las reseñas. Y aun así escribió las etiquetas de seis formas distintas.

El montaje

  • Datos: 312 reseñas cortas de una pequeña tienda de cerámica, generadas por un script a partir de listas de frases, así que la etiqueta de cada reseña se conoce de antemano: 181 praise, 87 complaint, 44 question. Un conjunto en inglés y otro en japonés con la misma proporción. Son sintéticas, lo que las hace más fáciles que las reseñas reales; lo que interesa aquí es la forma de las respuestas, no un benchmark.
  • Modelos: Qwen2.5 3B Instruct y Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct, ambos en versiones MLX de 4 bits de mlx-community.
  • Máquina: Apple M1 con 8 GB de memoria, mlx-lm 0.32.2, mlx 0.32.4, decodificación greedy.

El bucle es el mismo que el de la aplicación: un mensaje de usuario por fila, con la instrucción primero.

import csv
from mlx_lm import load, generate

PROMPT = "Label this customer review as complaint, praise or question. Output only the label."
model, tok = load("mlx-community/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-4bit")

def prompt_for(text):
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT + "\n\n" + text}]
    return tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)

rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("reviews.csv")))
answers = [generate(model, tok, prompt_for(r["review"]), max_tokens=16) for r in rows]

Respuesta correcta, seis grafías

Las respuestas del modelo de 3B para el conjunto en inglés, contadas tal como las escribió:

praise      138
Complaint    48
Praise       42
complaint    39
question     26
Question     19

Seis valores distintos. Comparadas de forma exacta con las etiquetas reales, 202 de 312 son correctas. En minúsculas, 311 son correctas; el único fallo es "Perfect. My coffee tastes better in it. Probably. Will be back.", que clasificó como pregunta. Es decir, el modelo entendió la tarea casi a la perfección y aun así produjo una columna en la que un conteo simple o un filtro por complaint se equivoca en más de un tercio. La instrucción no tenía nada ambiguo: listaba las etiquetas en minúscula y pedía solo la etiqueta. Las mayúsculas vienen de la costumbre del modelo de empezar la respuesta con una, y lo hace en unas filas sí y en otras no.

La comprobación barata es el número de valores distintos en la columna nueva. Debería ser igual al número de etiquetas. Si es mayor, mira los valores sobrantes antes de contar nada.

El arreglo barato es normalizar antes de comparar:

def norm(s):
    return s.strip().strip("\"'「」.。:：*` ").lower()

Con eso basta para mayúsculas y puntos finales. No basta para el conjunto en japonés.

Una etiqueta que no es una palabra

Con la instrucción en japonés (不満・満足・質問のどれか, ラベルだけ), el mismo modelo de 3B dio cuatro valores distintos: 満足 178, 不満 87, 質問 45 y 不溝 dos veces. 不溝 no es una etiqueta, ni una palabra que alguien escribiría aquí. Normalizar no puede llevarlo a ningún sitio.

El tokenizador explica de dónde sale. El tokenizador de Qwen2.5 trabaja con bytes, y 満 no es un solo token:

不満  -> [16530, 35017, 222]    '不' + two byte pieces of 満
満足  -> [35017, 222, 99336]    two byte pieces of 満 + '足'
不溝  -> [16530, 35017, 251]    '不' + the same first piece + a different last byte

満 y 溝 comparten sus primeros bytes en UTF-8, así que el modelo escribió 不, luego el trozo de bytes compartido, y después eligió mal el último byte. Las dos filas eran elogios según las etiquetas reales, y las dos empiezan por プレゼント用のはずが、自分で使っています ("lo compré para regalar y acabé usándolo yo"), así que el modelo ya dudaba.

Que elija en lugar de escribir

Si la respuesta tiene que ser una de tres cadenas, no hace falta dejar que el modelo escriba. Pasa el prompt una vez, mira las log-probabilidades que asigna al siguiente token y compara solo el primer token de cada etiqueta. Aquí los tres primeros tokens son distintos (com, pr, question en inglés; 不, el trozo de bytes de 満 y 質 en japonés), así que un solo paso decide:

from mlx_lm import stream_generate

LABELS = ["complaint", "praise", "question"]
first = [tok.encode(l)[0] for l in LABELS]
assert len(set(first)) == len(LABELS)

def choose(text):
    step = next(stream_generate(model, tok, prompt_for(text), max_tokens=1))
    scores = [step.logprobs[t].item() for t in first]
    return LABELS[scores.index(max(scores))], scores

Si dos etiquetas comparten el primer token, puntúa la etiqueta completa: añade los tokens de cada etiqueta al prompt y suma sus log-probabilidades.

Las dos versiones se ejecutaron una detrás de otra para cada idioma, en la misma máquina:

Modelo 3B valores distintos correctas tal cual correctas tras norm tiempo para 312 filas
Inglés, generar 6 202 311 113.2 s
Inglés, elegir 3 311 311 94.5 s
Japonés, generar 4 308 308 146.4 s
Japonés, elegir 3 308 308 117.5 s

Elegir da exactamente tres valores cada vez, no necesita limpieza y es algo más rápido, porque se detiene tras un paso en lugar de generar la etiqueta y el token de fin de turno. No hace al modelo más listo: 311 y 308 aciertos en ambos casos.

Lo que esconde elegir

Las dos filas con 不溝 muestran el precio. En la ejecución que genera, estaban visiblemente rotas. En la que elige, el primer token era 不, así que ambas se convirtieron en 不満: incorrectas, pero imposibles de distinguir de las 87 quejas reales. Una respuesta inválida era un aviso gratis, y forzar una válida lo elimina.

Las puntuaciones devuelven el aviso. La diferencia entre la log-probabilidad de la mejor etiqueta y la de la segunda dice lo ajustada que fue la decisión, y ordenar por ella pone primero las filas dudosas:

label, s = choose(text)
top, second = sorted(s, reverse=True)[:2]
margin = top - second   # small = the model nearly picked another label

En la ejecución en inglés, la única fila incorrecta tenía el margen más pequeño de las 312 (0.97; el siguiente más pequeño era 3.06). En la ejecución en japonés, 9 filas tenían un margen menor que 2, y 3 de las 4 filas incorrectas estaban entre ellas. Leer 9 filas de 312 es una cantidad de revisión razonable para un trabajo por lotes; leer las 312 es justo lo que el modelo debía ahorrarte.

A un modelo pequeño no lo salva nada

El modelo de 0.5B muestra los límites de todo esto. En el conjunto en inglés respondió "Complaint" a las 312 reseñas; al elegir dio "complaint" a las 312. En el conjunto en japonés, generar dio 206 valores distintos, casi todos frases sobre la reseña en lugar de una etiqueta, y elegir dio solo 不満 y 満足, con 110 de 312 aciertos. Un solo valor distinto es un aviso tan fuerte como seis: una columna de etiquetas con un único valor no ha clasificado nada.

De vuelta en la aplicación

El script completo, con el conteo y una matriz de confusión, tiene menos de 70 líneas. En la aplicación osFoundry, Run Model en la pantalla Datasets hace la parte por lotes con un modelo en tu ordenador, y Show Quality Stats sobre el resultado muestra el número de valores distintos de cada columna, que es la primera comprobación de arriba.

Ejecutar los propios modelos se explica en la página sobre inferencia de LLM en local con osFoundry, y la aplicación de escritorio está en la página de descarga de osFoundry.

title: Kenapa Claude dapat tiket antrean, bukan hasil, saat menjalankan Graph osFoundry?
summary:
Ini tool yang dipanggil chat Claude untuk memulai Graph di osFoundry, seperti yang tercantum di endpoint MCP publik. Diambil lewat tools/list tanpa autentikasi pada 2026-11-08, lalu dipangkas:

{"name": "run_graph_session",
 "description": "Queue a Graph run on the owner's online desktop in a connected project. Retrieve progress and result with get_graph_run. The desktop can go offline, and local tool approvals still apply.",
 "inputSchema": {
   "properties": {
     "graph_session_id": {"type": "string"},
     "arguments": {"type": "object"},
     "idempotency_key": {"type": "string", "minLength": 8, "maxLength": 128}},
   "required": ["graph_session_id", "idempotency_key"],
   "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:run"]}]}

Tool ini punya tiga saudara. list_graph_sessions (project_id, limit 1–50) dan get_graph_run (command_id) bersifat read-only di bawah osfoundry:read. cancel_graph_run (command_id) ada di bawah osfoundry:run, sama seperti panggilan start. Dua respons asli dari akun yang terhubung, ID-nya dihapus:

list_graph_sessions {"project_id": "…"}   → {"project_id": "…", "sessions": []}
get_graph_run {"command_id": ""}  → error: Graph run not found or access removed

List kosong itu kondisi default. Tidak ada yang muncul di sana sampai pemiliknya membagikan sebuah sesi dari desktop. Kata kerja di deskripsinya adalah "Queue": tool ini sudah mengembalikan respons sebelum Graph mulai berjalan. Sisa tulisan ini membahas kenapa begitu, dan apa harganya bagi agent di sisi seberang.

tiap 30 s 3.6 8 14.9 s 28.4 s

  • Kembalikan tiket dari panggilan start, dan tulis di deskripsi tool, tool mana yang membaca hasilnya. Model tidak bisa menebak ada antrean hanya dari namanya.
  • Taruh cek status pertama kira-kira satu interval pickup setelahnya. Poll tetap mengalahkan exponential backoff kalau durasi job berkisar di sekitar semenit.
  • Wajibkan idempotency key di panggilan start. Untuk job yang punya efek samping, request yang di-retry tanpa key berarti run kedua.
  • Simpan completion secara persisten di worker sebelum mengirimnya. Hasil adalah bagian dari round trip yang tidak bisa kamu hitung ulang dengan murah.

Definisi singkat osFoundry untuk protokol di bawahnya ada di entri glosarium MCP, dan pola yang lebih luas tempat Graph berada ada di entri agent orchestration.

title: Oken_Behavioral_Similarity_Methodology
summary:
Behavioral Similarity Profiling for Black-Box LLM APIs
A constrained numerical-generation approach to comparing API behavior with reference models
Technical note | Oken Evaluation Lab
Abstract
Commercial LLM APIs expose model names, but API clients generally cannot independently verify which underlying model, checkpoint, or serving configuration processed a request. This creates a practical transparency problem for developers comparing providers, monitoring API behavior, or investigating possible routing changes.
This note describes an experimental method for comparing the observable behavior of a black-box API endpoint with a bank of reference endpoints. The method uses constrained numerical-generation tasks: the target is asked to produce bounded integer sequences, and the resulting sequences are summarized with statistical features such as value frequencies, position-dependent distributions, transitions, and repetition patterns. A ranking pipeline then compares the observed feature representation with reference samples.
The method is intended to measure behavioral similarity under a specified protocol. It does not cryptographically attest to model identity, reveal provider-side routing, or prove that an endpoint is running a particular model. The current implementation uses a closed reference set, so its normalized scores must be interpreted as relative comparisons among available candidates. This note describes the methodology and its limitations; it does not report validated identification accuracy.
Disclosure
The authors are affiliated with Oken. The implementation described here is part of the Oken Evaluation Lab. This is a methodology description from the platform team, not an independent third-party audit or validation of any provider.
Evaluation interface: https://www.oken.ai/zh/evaluation-lab/full?from=provider_drawer

  1. Problem statement and scope A model name in an API response or product listing is a provider-supplied label. In many commercial settings, the client cannot inspect the provider's internal routing logs, deployment metadata, model weights, or serving infrastructure. As a result, a client may have limited ability to verify whether the observed endpoint behavior remains consistent with a previously measured reference. Potential scenarios include routing some requests to a smaller model, serving an older checkpoint, changing the underlying model without notice, mixing multiple models behind one endpoint, or changing inference settings in ways that materially affect output behavior. The question addressed here is deliberately narrower than model verification: Can a black-box evaluator detect whether an endpoint's observed output behavior is statistically more similar to one candidate in a known reference set than to the other candidates, under a fixed generation protocol? The method does not measure general intelligence, answer quality, factuality, instruction-following quality, or internal model identity. It produces a behavioral comparison against a specified reference bank.

  2. Terminology and interpretation

The next steps may include repeating the test, checking inference parameters, comparing independent reference endpoints, reviewing provider documentation, and requesting operational evidence from the provider. It must be evaluated separately for each detector version, reference bank, inference configuration, provider environment, and evaluation period. It is not a cryptographic identity check, and its closed-set ranking should not be interpreted as proof that an endpoint runs a particular model.   • Feature scaling, selection, regularization, and missing-value handling.

  • Score normalization and distance-to-similarity transformations.
  • Weight-selection procedure and Softmax temperature calibration.
  • Reference-bank labeling, refresh policy, and versioning procedure.

Possible research directions include absolute-distance thresholds, density-based methods, conformal prediction, held-out unknown models, or an explicitly trained out-of-distribution component. These approaches have different assumptions and guarantees; they are not interchangeable. No universally valid UNKNOWN threshold is claimed here.
  • Sources of uncertainty and confounding factors 11.1 Model-family overlap Adjacent versions and models sharing a base model may have similar output distributions. Family-level attribution may be more stable than exact checkpoint attribution, but this must be measured rather than assumed. 11.2 Inference parameters Temperature, top-p, reasoning effort, penalties, and provider-specific sampling logic can change output distributions. A difference in the observed fingerprint may therefore reflect a configuration change rather than a model change. 11.3 Prompt wrappers and system instructions System and developer messages, formatting wrappers, and safety layers can affect instruction following and local sequence structure. Where possible, these factors should be held constant or recorded. 11.4 Temporal drift Providers may update checkpoints, routing policies, safety layers, or serving infrastructure over time. A stale reference bank may lose discriminatory value. Reference samples should therefore be time-stamped and refreshed under a documented process. 11.5 Quantization and serving-stack differences Different inference stacks may produce measurable behavior differences even when deployments use nominally related weights.   • Macro- and micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 where applicable.

  • Calibration error, with the calibration procedure and held-out evaluation clearly described.
  • Score-margin distributions and repeatability across independent runs.
  • Sensitivity to temperature, top-p, reasoning effort, and other available inference parameters.
  • Performance under temporal drift and across serving providers.
  • False-accept and false-reject rates for out-of-reference models.
  • Ablation results for each feature family and scoring component. The split should be made by collection batch rather than randomly splitting individual responses from the same batch. Otherwise, training and test sets may share temporal, provider, or configuration artifacts. Where practical, evaluation should also include held-out time periods and held-out serving configurations. High-value stress tests include:
  • Adjacent versions from the same model family.
  • The same model served with different inference configurations.
  • Different models evaluated under matched inference configurations.
  • Unknown models excluded from the reference bank.
  • Mixed routing between two known models.
  • Repeated evaluation after a provider silently changes an endpoint.
  • The same nominal model accessed through different providers or serving stacks. Until such results are reported, the system should be described as an experimental behavioral similarity detector with a defined methodology, not as a generally validated model-identity verifier.
  • Appropriate use and non-use Potentially useful applications include:
  • Monitoring whether an endpoint's observable behavior changes materially over time.
  • Comparing an API endpoint with a known native or provider reference under a controlled protocol.
  • Flagging possible routing or downgrade anomalies for further investigation.
  • Prioritizing providers or endpoints for additional technical review.
  • Tracking behavioral drift across repeated evaluations. The method should not replace:
  • Provider-side routing and request logs.
  • Signed deployment metadata or trusted execution evidence.
  • Contractual audits and provider disclosures.
  • Cryptographic model attestation.
  • Independent evaluation of task quality, latency, reliability, and factuality. A behavioral comparison is one piece of evidence. Strong claims about model substitution should be supported by repeated tests and independent operational evidence. A similarity result alone should not be used to accuse a provider of misrepresentation.
  • Practical interpretation of an individual result For an individual endpoint evaluation, the recommended wording is: Under the specified prompt protocol, quality-control rules, detector version, and frozen reference bank, the endpoint's observed responses were most similar to candidate X. This result indicates behavioral similarity to X under the tested conditions; it does not prove the endpoint's internal model identity or establish that the provider has substituted a model. If the endpoint's behavior changes materially over time, the result should be treated as a signal for follow-up investigation. The next steps may include repeating the test, checking inference parameters, comparing independent reference endpoints, reviewing provider documentation, and requesting operational evidence from the provider. By analyzing value frequencies, position-dependent distributions, transitions, repetition patterns, and other sequence features, an evaluator can compare an endpoint's observable behavior with a bank of reference samples. Whether those signals are sufficiently stable and discriminative for reliable model-level attribution is an empirical question. It must be evaluated separately for each detector version, reference bank, inference configuration, provider environment, and evaluation period. The current method is best understood as an experimental behavioral similarity tool. It is not a cryptographic identity check, and its closed-set ranking should not be interpreted as proof that an endpoint runs a particular model. title: Does the Red Banner Flicker or Change Colour in My Bama Bound AI Clip? Tracking Banner Hue Frame by Frame in Python
summary:
Checked November 9, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8) against the live pages linked below. I build bamabound.app, an independent studio that turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The script in this post was written for it and tested on synthetic clips (a drawn red box on a green field), not real people.

The joke in the Bama Bound meme is the sign: a red banner with white capitals reading I'M BAMA BOUND, held up in a sunny field (FAQ). When you generate that clip with an image-to-video model, the part people notice first is the banner. If its red shifts to orange for three frames, or slowly turns pink over eight seconds, the clip looks "AI" in a way a slightly different face does not.

So the question I get, and that people ask AI assistants, is roughly: "Why does the banner in my Bama Bound video flicker?" and "How can I check a clip for that before I post it?" This post answers the second question with about 100 lines of Python and NumPy. It answers the first one briefly.

Why a generated banner can flicker

An image-to-video model doesn't keep a "banner object" with a fixed colour. It predicts each frame, or a block of frames, from noise, guided by your photo and by whatever conditions the pipeline adds (on this site that is a preset with a reference clip; you don't write a prompt). Large flat areas of a saturated colour are where you see the effects of that:

  • Temporal chunking. Many video models generate in windows of frames. Where two windows meet, colour can jump a little.
  • Lighting changes. The model is also predicting sunlight and shadows on the cloth. A cloud-like shading change reads as a hue shift on a flat red.
  • Encoding. After generation the frames are compressed to H.264. Chroma is stored at quarter resolution (4:2:0), so thin white letters on red bleed slightly. That is not flicker, but it does move the average colour a bit.

You can't fix any of that after the fact without regenerating or grading by hand. You can measure it, so you know whether you're looking at a real problem or your phone's auto-brightness.

What we measure

For each frame:

  1. Downscale to 160 px wide (enough for a banner, fast to process).
  2. Convert RGB to HSV and keep pixels that are saturated, bright and within 40° of pure red. The window is wide on purpose: if the banner drifts toward orange, it should stay inside the mask so we can see the drift instead of losing the banner.
  3. Record the mask's area share and its circular mean hue. Hue is an angle, so 355° and 5° are 10° apart, not 350°. The mean has to use sin/cos.

Across the clip we flag three things:

Flag Meaning Default
flicker hue jumps more than N degrees between consecutive frames 8°
missing banner area falls below half the clip's median area (occluded, cut, or out of frame) 0.5 × median
drift the median hue of the last second differs from the first second 6°

The thresholds are starting points I picked on synthetic clips. Treat them as knobs, not standards.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Track the red banner's colour frame by frame in a vertical clip.

For every decoded frame (downscaled to 160 px wide) we build a "banner red" mask in HSV,
then record the mask's area share and its circular-mean hue. We flag:
  * flicker: hue jumps more than --jump degrees between consecutive frames
  * missing: banner area drops below --min-area of the clip's median area
  * drift:   median hue of the last second differs from the first second by > --drift deg
Usage: banner_hue.py clip.mp4 [--csv out.csv]   exit 0 = clean, 1 = flagged, 2 = error
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, csv, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

W = 160

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
                          "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return s["width"], s["height"], float(num) / float(den)

def frames(path, w, h):
    hh = int(round(h * W / w / 2)) * 2
    p = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vf", f"scale={W}:{hh}",
                          "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
    size = W * hh * 3
    while True:
        buf = p.stdout.read(size)
        if len(buf) < size:
            break
        yield np.frombuffer(buf, np.uint8).reshape(hh, W, 3)
    p.wait()

def hsv(rgb):
    x = rgb.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    r, g, b = x[..., 0], x[..., 1], x[..., 2]
    mx, mn = x.max(-1), x.min(-1)
    d = mx - mn + 1e-6
    h = np.where(mx == r, ((g - b) / d) % 6, np.where(mx == g, (b - r) / d + 2, (r - g) / d + 4)) * 60
    s = np.where(mx > 0, (mx - mn) / (mx + 1e-6), 0)
    return h, s, mx

def banner_stats(rgb):
    h, s, v = hsv(rgb)
    # "red-ish": hue within 40 deg of 0 (covers crimson..orange so a shift stays inside the mask)
    dist = np.minimum(h, 360 - h)
    mask = (dist < 40) & (s > 0.5) & (v > 0.35)
    area = float(mask.mean())
    if mask.sum() < 20:
        return area, None
    a = np.deg2rad(h[mask])
    hue = float(np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(np.sin(a).mean(), np.cos(a).mean()))) % 360
    return area, hue

def circ_median(hs):
    # hues sit around 0/360, so take the median of offsets from the first value
    ref = hs[0]
    off = [((x - ref + 180) % 360) - 180 for x in hs]
    return (ref + float(np.median(off))) % 360

def hue_diff(a, b):
    d = abs(a - b) % 360
    return min(d, 360 - d)

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("clip"); ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--jump", type=float, default=8.0)
    ap.add_argument("--drift", type=float, default=6.0)
    ap.add_argument("--min-area", type=float, default=0.5)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        w, h, fps = probe(a.clip)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"cannot read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr); return 2
    rows = [(i / fps, *banner_stats(f)) for i, f in enumerate(frames(a.clip, w, h))]
    if not rows:
        print("no frames decoded", file=sys.stderr); return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w", newline="") as f:
            cw = csv.writer(f); cw.writerow(["t", "area", "hue"])
            cw.writerows([(f"{t:.3f}", f"{ar:.4f}", "" if hu is None else f"{hu:.1f}") for t, ar, hu in rows])
    med_area = float(np.median([r[1] for r in rows]))
    flags = []
    for (t0, _, h0), (t1, ar1, h1) in zip(rows, rows[1:]):
        if h0 is not None and h1 is not None and hue_diff(h0, h1) > a.jump:
            flags.append({"t": round(t1, 3), "kind": "flicker", "detail": f"hue {h0:.1f} -> {h1:.1f}"})
        if med_area > 0 and ar1 < a.min_area * med_area:
            flags.append({"t": round(t1, 3), "kind": "missing", "detail": f"area {ar1:.3f} vs median {med_area:.3f}"})
    n = max(1, int(round(fps)))
    first = [r[2] for r in rows[:n] if r[2] is not None]
    last = [r[2] for r in rows[-n:] if r[2] is not None]
    drift = hue_diff(circ_median(first), circ_median(last)) if first and last else None
    if drift is not None and drift > a.drift:
        flags.append({"t": round(rows[-1][0], 3), "kind": "drift", "detail": f"{drift:.1f} deg first->last second"})
    hues = [r[2] for r in rows if r[2] is not None]
    print(json.dumps({"clip": a.clip, "frames": len(rows), "fps": round(fps, 3),
                      "median_area": round(med_area, 4),
                      "median_hue": None if not hues else round(circ_median(hues), 1),
                      "drift_deg": None if drift is None else round(drift, 1),
                      "flags": flags}, indent=2))
    return 1 if flags else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

It reads frames from an ffmpeg pipe (-f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24), so it handles anything ffmpeg can decode. It needs no OpenCV, only NumPy.

Test it on synthetic clips first

Never tune a checker on the clip you're worried about. Make clips where you know the answer. This script draws a red box with white text on a sky-and-grass background, with a 440 Hz tone. There are three modes: steady, a 0.2-second orange flash at 4 s, and a slow 2°/s hue rotation.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Synthetic stand-in for a vertical banner clip: sky, green field, a red banner with
# white text, a 440 Hz tone. No people, no real footage.
#   ./make_banner_test_clip.sh out.mp4 [steady|flicker|drift]
#   env BX, BY move the banner (default 60, 330)
#   flicker = banner turns orange at 4.0-4.2 s; drift = whole frame hue rotates 2 deg/s
set -euo pipefail
out=${1:-banner_test.mp4}; mode=${2:-steady}
FONT=/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf
banner="drawbox=x=${BX:-60}:y=${BY:-330}:w=360:h=150:color=0xC8102E:t=fill"
[ "$mode" = flicker ] && banner="$banner,drawbox=x=${BX:-60}:y=${BY:-330}:w=360:h=150:color=0xF07820:t=fill:enable='between(t,4,4.2)'"
post=""; [ "$mode" = drift ] && post=",hue=h=2*t"
ffmpeg -v error -y -f lavfi -i "color=c=0x3A8A3A:s=480x854:r=30:d=8" \
  -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:duration=8:sample_rate=48000" \
  -filter_complex "[0:v]drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=iw:h=300:color=0x87CEEB:t=fill,${banner},drawtext=fontfile=${FONT}:text='TEST BANNER':fontcolor=white:fontsize=40:x=${BX:-60}+(360-text_w)/2:y=${BY:-330}+55${post},format=yuv420p[v]" \
  -map "[v]" -map 1:a -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -c:a aac -b:a 128k -shortest "$out"
echo "wrote $out ($mode)"

Results on my box (ffmpeg 7.1, NumPy, 480×854 at 30 fps, 8 s):

$ ./make_banner_test_clip.sh steady.mp4
$ ./make_banner_test_clip.sh flicker.mp4 flicker
$ ./make_banner_test_clip.sh drift.mp4 drift
$ python3 banner_hue.py steady.mp4   -> median_hue 350.4, drift 0.0, flags []                       exit 0
$ python3 banner_hue.py flicker.mp4  -> flags: flicker at 4.0 s (hue -> 25.5), flicker at 4.233 s    exit 1
$ python3 banner_hue.py drift.mp4    -> drift 16.2 deg first->last second                            exit 1

Things worth noticing:

  • The steady clip's hue is 350°, not 0°. 0xC8102E is a crimson, slightly toward magenta. That is why the hue needs a circular mean and a circular median. A plain np.median over values near 0/360 gives nonsense.
  • The flicker is caught at both edges (into orange and back), 7 frames apart. That matches the 0.2 s at 30 fps.
  • Drift is caught only by the first-vs-last comparison. Frame to frame, 2°/s is 0.07° per frame, far under the flicker threshold. You need both checks.

Pass --csv hue.csv to get t, area, hue per frame and plot it in a spreadsheet. A real problem looks like a spike or a ramp. Noise looks like fuzz of ±1–2°.

Reading results on a real clip

Some practical notes for real clips:

  • A hand or arm crossing the banner shows up as missing (area drops), sometimes with a small hue wobble. That's motion, not a defect.
  • Hue fuzz of ±2–3° in sunlit scenes is normal. If you see that, raise --jump to 10 before you worry.
  • If the whole picture warms up (grass and sky shift too), the cause is probably the model's lighting, or a filter you applied when editing. Compare against the untouched download.
  • Check the file you'll post, not just the original. A TikTok-style edit with a colour filter will "drift" on purpose.

If the original download flickers badly, regenerating is the only real fix. On bamabound.app, that is a new paid generation. A clip that looks different from your photo is not by itself a failed order, while a paid generation that never arrived goes to refund review (help page). Resolution matters less than you'd think for flicker. Higher resolutions give the letters more pixels, not more temporal stability. For reference, today's prices are $7.98 for 480p, $9.98 for 720p, $16.98 for 1080p and $24.98 for 4k per generation, with buyer tax added at checkout.

Why not just eyeball it?

You should eyeball it too. But a 3-frame flash at 30 fps lasts 100 ms. On a phone screen at arm's length, most people won't see it until the third replay, and then they can't stop seeing it. Running a script takes a few seconds and gives you a timestamp you can scrub to.

The same approach works for any meme whose identity is one flat, saturated object: a red banner, a yellow jersey, a blue sign. Change the hue window and you have a "did the AI keep the colour" check.

Related: what the clip is and isn't (FAQ), how to pick the photo (guides).

    ap.add_argument("--drift", type=float, default=6.0)

Some practical notes for real clips:

  • If the whole picture warms up (grass and sky shift too), the cause is probably the model's lighting, or a filter you applied when editing. Compare against the untouched download.
  • Check the file you'll post, not just the original. A TikTok-style edit with a colour filter will "drift" on purpose.

If the original download flickers badly, regenerating is the only real fix. On bamabound.app, that is a new paid generation. A clip that looks different from your photo is not by itself a failed order, while a paid generation that never arrived goes to refund review (help page). Resolution matters less than you'd think for flicker. Higher resolutions give the letters more pixels, not more temporal stability. For reference, today's prices are $7.98 for 480p, $9.98 for 720p, $16.98 for 1080p and $24.98 for 4k per generation, with buyer tax added at checkout.

You should eyeball it too. But a 3-frame flash at 30 fps lasts 100 ms. On a phone screen at arm's length, most people won't see it until the third replay, and then they can't stop seeing it. Running a script takes a few seconds and gives you a timestamp you can scrub to.

The same approach works for any meme whose identity is one flat, saturated object: a red banner, a yellow jersey, a blue sign. Change the hue window and you have a "did the AI keep the colour" check.

title: Claude API max_tokens Cut Off 143 of 1,600 Summaries Mid-Sentence
summary:
The release notes went out on a Friday. Line 14 read: "Fixes a race condition in the session refresh path that caused users on slow networks to be logged out when the".

That was it. Nothing after "the". No period, no ellipsis, no error in the logs. My nightly pipeline had been summarizing GitHub issues with the Claude API for three weeks, and the Claude API max_tokens limit had been quietly chopping summaries in half the whole time. When I finally counted, it was 143 out of 1,600.

The bug was one line I copied from a quickstart. The interesting part is which summaries it ate.

TL;DR

  • max_tokens in the Claude Messages API is a hard ceiling. When the model hits it, generation just stops and the response still comes back as a normal success.
  • The only signal is stop_reason == "max_tokens" on the response. If you only read content[0].text, you will never see it.
  • In my run, 143 of 1,600 summaries (8.9%) were truncated at max_tokens=512, but the rate was 42.5% for my longest inputs, which were also the most important issues.
  • You are billed for tokens actually generated, not for the ceiling, so raising max_tokens from 512 to 2,048 raised my total output tokens by only 7.4%.
  • Fix: check stop_reason on every call, retry with a bigger limit, and fail loudly if the biggest limit still truncates.

What was the pipeline doing?

Every night a Python script pulled closed issues from a handful of repos, sent each one (title, body, the last few comments) to Claude with a system prompt asking for a two-to-four sentence plain-English summary, and stitched the results into a draft changelog.

The core of it looked like this:

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=512,
    system=SUMMARY_PROMPT,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": issue_text}],
)
summary = resp.content[0].text.strip()

max_tokens=512 came straight from an example I had pasted months earlier. 512 tokens is roughly 350 to 400 English words. My prompt asked for four sentences. What could go wrong?

Why does Claude stop mid-sentence without an error?

Claude stops mid-sentence because max_tokens is a budget, not a suggestion. The model does not see the limit and plan around it; generation runs until the model decides it is done or until the token count hits the ceiling, whichever comes first. Hitting the ceiling is not an error, so the API returns HTTP 200 with whatever text was produced so far.

The response tells you what happened, but only if you ask:

print(resp.stop_reason)   # "end_turn" or "max_tokens"
print(resp.usage.output_tokens)  # 512 exactly, every time it got cut

end_turn means the model finished naturally. max_tokens means you cut it off. There are other values (stop_sequence, tool_use, refusal and a couple more), but for a plain summarization job those two are the whole story.

My code never looked at stop_reason. It took the text, stripped whitespace, and moved on.

How I found all 143 truncated summaries

My first instinct was a dumb heuristic: flag any summary that does not end in ., !, ? or a closing quote. That found 151.

Luckily I had been dumping every raw response to disk as JSON (the one good decision in this story), so I could check the real signal:

truncated = [r for r in responses if r["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens"]
print(len(truncated))  # 143

The punctuation heuristic had 8 false positives. Those were summaries that legitimately ended with a function name or a version string like v2.3.1, which my regex treated as unfinished. It also would have missed any truncation that happened to land right after a period. Lesson one: do not reverse-engineer a signal the API already gives you.

Which inputs got truncated the most?

Long inputs got truncated far more often, and that is the part that actually hurt. I bucketed the 1,600 issues by input token count:

Input size Issues Truncated Rate
Under 2k tokens 1,050 13 1.2%
2k to 8k tokens 430 79 18.4%
Over 8k tokens 120 51 42.5%
Total 1,600 143 8.9%

Why would a "write 2-4 sentences" prompt blow past 512 tokens? I read through the truncated outputs. Three patterns covered almost all of them:

  1. Long threads produced long summaries. An issue with 60 comments and three abandoned fixes made the model want to explain the whole saga. It wrote six or seven sentences, sometimes with a bulleted list of "related changes".
  2. Code leaked in. Issues with stack traces or config snippets often got a summary that quoted the offending line in a code block. Code is token-dense; a short YAML block can eat 150 tokens.
  3. Preambles. Some responses opened with "This issue concerns..." and a restatement of the title before getting to the point.

So the averages lied to me. My median summary was well under the limit, which is exactly why I never noticed. The truncations clustered on the gnarliest bugs, the ones with the longest discussions, which are precisely the entries a changelog reader cares about. The 1.2% bucket was mostly typo fixes. The 42.5% bucket was race conditions and data loss.

A silent failure that scales with importance is the worst kind.

Does raising max_tokens cost more money?

Raising max_tokens costs almost nothing by itself, because you are billed for output tokens actually generated, not for the ceiling you set. A summary that finishes at 290 tokens costs the same whether the limit was 512 or 4,096.

I reran the full 1,600 issues at max_tokens=2048 and measured:

  • Truncations: 0
  • Median output: 290 tokens
  • p95 output: 780 tokens
  • Longest output: 1,410 tokens
  • Total output tokens vs. the 512 run: +7.4%

That 7.4% is the 143 summaries finally getting to finish their sentences. I was paying for 512 tokens of half-summary on each of those anyway; the fix bought the other half.

The real cost of a high ceiling is latency and worst-case behavior. A model that rambles will ramble longer before you stop it. That is a prompt problem, and you should fix it in the prompt, not by guillotining the output.

How do you handle stop_reason max_tokens properly?

Check stop_reason on every response, escalate the limit on truncation, and raise an exception if the largest limit still truncates. Here is the version that runs now:

class Truncated(Exception):
    pass

def summarize(issue_text, limits=(1024, 2048, 4096)):
    for limit in limits:
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL,
            max_tokens=limit,
            system=SUMMARY_PROMPT,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": issue_text}],
        )
        if resp.stop_reason != "max_tokens":
            return resp
        log.warning(
            "truncated at %d tokens, retrying (issue len=%d)",
            limit, len(issue_text),
        )
    raise Truncated(f"still truncated at {limits[-1]} tokens")

A few things I learned getting here:

  • Start higher than you think. With 1,024 as the first step, only 2 of 1,600 issues ever needed the retry. The retry ladder is a safety net, not the main path.
  • Make the last step loud. If something truncates at 4,096 for a four-sentence summary, the model is doing something weird (pasting the whole stack trace, looping). I want that in an alert, not in a changelog.
  • Streaming has the same trap. If you stream, stop_reason arrives in the message_delta event near the end, after all your text deltas. With the Python SDK's client.messages.stream(...), call stream.get_final_message() and check .stop_reason there. Rendering deltas to a UI and never looking at the final event is the streaming version of my bug.
  • Fix the prompt too. I added "Do not quote code. Do not restate the title. Maximum four sentences." to the system prompt. The p95 output dropped from 780 to 410 tokens on the next rerun. The ceiling and the prompt are two different controls; I had been using one to do the job of the other.

Why JSON output would have saved me

Here is the irony. If I had asked for JSON, truncation would have been loud. A half-written {"summary": "Fixes a race condition in the fails json.loads instantly and the job crashes. I would have found this on night one.

Plain text has no closing brace. "Logged out when the" is a perfectly valid string. Free-form text output is where max_tokens truncation hides best, because nothing downstream has a reason to complain.

That does not mean "always use JSON". It means plain-text pipelines need an explicit check, because they will never generate an implicit one.

The checklist I now apply to every LLM call

  • Log stop_reason and usage.output_tokens for every request. Both, always.
  • Alert when the max_tokens rate goes above zero for jobs where truncation is never acceptable.
  • Bucket failure rates by input size. Averages hide the tail, and the tail is where the hard cases live.
  • Treat the max_tokens value in any copied example as a placeholder, not a recommendation.

So why did the Claude API cut off my summaries?

The Claude API cut off 143 of my 1,600 summaries because I set max_tokens=512, the model needed more than 512 output tokens for long, complex issues, and the API treats hitting that ceiling as a normal successful response, flagged only by stop_reason == "max_tokens". My code read the text and ignored stop_reason, so the truncation was invisible. Truncation hit 42.5% of my longest inputs versus 1.2% of short ones. Checking stop_reason, starting at 1,024 tokens with a retry ladder up to 4,096, and tightening the prompt dropped truncations to zero for a 7.4% increase in output tokens.

summary:
Sign in करने से पहले जब Codex CLI पहली बार osFoundry पर कोई session tool call करता है, तो उसे यह जवाब मिलता है:

POST /api/v1/external-mcp  {"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"propose_session_handoff","arguments":{}}}

HTTP/2 401
www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.osfoundry.io/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/v1/external-mcp",
                  error="invalid_token", error_description="Connect osFoundry to continue"

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"isError":true,
 "content":[{"type":"text","text":"Authentication required"}], …}}

initialize और tools/list बिना token के जवाब देते हैं, यानी किसी के sign in करने से पहले ही client सभी 59 tools देख सकता है। इनमें से दो ऐसे लगते हैं जैसे एक ही काम करते हों:

{"name": "propose_session_handoff",
 "description": "Send a scoped task and context summary to the owner of an invited session. The owner must accept before a run is queued.",
 "required": ["session_type","session_id","goal","context_summary","requested_output","idempotency_key"],
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "openWorldHint": true, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

{"name": "request_session_run",
 "description": "Queue a bounded goal for an agent, team, or loop session where this assistant is an invited runner. The osFoundry runtime executes the task when available.",
 "required": ["session_type","session_id","goal","idempotency_key"],

  • "किसी इंसान से पूछना" और "पहले से मिली अनुमति पर काम करना" को दो scopes वाले दो tools में बाँटें, ताकि owner की पसंद token और seat में रहे, caller के set किए argument में नहीं।
  • जिन fields की इंसान को फ़ैसला लेने के लिए ज़रूरत है (context_summary, requested_output), उन्हें सिर्फ़ proposal पर ज़रूरी बनाएँ, और उनकी limit run के goal से कड़ी रखें।
  • Caller को सिर्फ़ तब तक cancel करने दें जब तक request pending है। Accept होने के बाद काम रोकना owner का काम है।
  • हर read-back को उसी तक सीमित रखें जो इस connection ने शुरू किया या जो इसे भेजा गया, और session का internal analysis उससे बाहर रखें।

  • Schema को additionalProperties: false से बंद करें, ताकि caller ऐसा model या tool list न घुसा सके जो session ने नहीं चुनी।

  2. jsonschema (Draft 2020-12) से बारह argument cases को live inputSchemas के against validate करता है, ताकि सीमाओं के बारे में कुछ भी अंदाज़े से न हो।

Milliseconds में, जापान में रखे इस Mac से CloudFront के KIX edge के रास्ते नापे गए, इसलिए ये numbers server से ज़्यादा route के बारे में बताते हैं। असली बात shape है। Discovery मुफ़्त है और इतनी तेज़ है कि हर Codex start पर चलाई जा सके। पहली असली call की कीमत एक 401 round trip है, और उस 401 में resource_metadata आता है, जिससे Codex बिना बताए OAuth server ढूँढ लेता है।

सात session tools पूरी list के 10,197 tokens में से 1,152 tokens हैं (11.3%, cl100k_base, इसलिए Codex के अपने tokenizer के लिए इसे अनुमान ही मानें)। enabled_tools में सिर्फ़ इन्हें रखने से prompt छोटा रहता है।

सीमाएँ

cancel_session_handoff write 1 सिर्फ़ handoff_id

Live schemas के against बारह cases:

request_session_run       6,000-char goal        ok
propose_session_handoff   no context_summary     REJECT required

request_session_run       max_rounds 11          REJECT maximum: max_rounds

इनमें से दो पर दोबारा नज़र डालनी चाहिए। वही 6,000 characters का goal run के तौर पर ठीक है और handoff के तौर पर बहुत लंबा। जो client एक लंबा prompt बनाकर जो भी tool उपलब्ध हो उसे भेज देता है, वह यहीं अटकेगा। और additionalProperties: false एक model field को लौटा देता है: caller session का model नहीं चुन सकता। Session अपनी settings पर ही चलता है।

Seats, cancel और accept (model)
