यह matrix Connected tab के help text को table में बदलकर बनाया गया है। दिलचस्प rule cancel window का है। cancel_session_handoff की description के मुताबिक यह "before its owner accepts it" काम करता है, यानी जो पहले हो, वही जीतता है। एक बार run queue में चला गया, तो उसे वापस लेना caller के हाथ में नहीं रहता। इसी वजह से cancel सिर्फ़ एक handoff_id लेता है: कोई state भेजनी नहीं है, बस एक pending row बंद करनी है।

खोए हुए responses

हर write में idempotency_key ज़रूरी है। इससे क्या मिलता है, यह देखने के लिए model 1,000 request_session_run calls भेजता है, 20% responses गिरा देता है (seed 7) और client को उसी key के साथ तीन बार तक retry करने देता है:

server honours idempotency_key=True  calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1000  duplicates 0
server honours idempotency_key=False calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1276  duplicates 276

किसी और के runtime पर 276 extra runs, ठीक इसी case के लिए key ज़रूरी रखी गई है। Timeout के बाद retry करने वाला हर client इससे टकराएगा, और जो run पहले ही शुरू हो चुका है, उसे आप दो बार नहीं चाहेंगे। Key को optional की जगह required रखने का मतलब है कि कोई client उसे भूल नहीं सकता।

पूरी script को Apple M1 पर 26.4 s wall-clock time लगा। लगभग सारा समय 45 network calls में गया, और user CPU time 0.37 s था।

अगर आप इसे खुद wire करें

  • "किसी इंसान से पूछना" और "पहले से मिली अनुमति पर काम करना" को दो scopes वाले दो tools में बाँटें, ताकि owner की पसंद token और seat में रहे, caller के set किए argument में नहीं।
  • जिन fields की इंसान को फ़ैसला लेने के लिए ज़रूरत है (context_summary, requested_output), उन्हें सिर्फ़ proposal पर ज़रूरी बनाएँ, और उनकी limit run के goal से कड़ी रखें।
  • Caller को सिर्फ़ तब तक cancel करने दें जब तक request pending है। Accept होने के बाद काम रोकना owner का काम है।
  • हर read-back को उसी तक सीमित रखें जो इस connection ने शुरू किया या जो इसे भेजा गया, और session का internal analysis उससे बाहर रखें।
  • हर write पर idempotency_key ज़रूरी बनाएँ, और repeat होने पर पहला result लौटाएँ।
  • Schema को additionalProperties: false से बंद करें, ताकि caller ऐसा model या tool list न घुसा सके जो session ने नहीं चुनी।

osFoundry के अपने agents steps के बीच काम कैसे आगे बढ़ाते हैं, यह handoffs page पर है। नीचे के protocol के लिए MCP glossary entry देखें।

title: Pull Agoda hotel reviews with scores and sub-scores into a spreadsheet, in Python
summary:
If you manage a hotel, run a reputation-management tool or analyse a city's hotel market, Agoda is one of the review sources you can't skip in Asia. A single hotel page there mixes two review pools: reviews from Agoda's own guests and reviews from Booking.com guests that Agoda republishes. Each pool has its own score, its own review count and its own six sub-scores (cleanliness, facilities, location, room comfort, service, value for money).

Reading that by hand works for one property. For a competitive set of 20 hotels, checked every morning, it doesn't. This post pulls the reviews and scores into a CSV in Python and shows a daily "new reviews only" setup.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Agoda API, an Agoda reviews scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What each row holds

One row per review, from the hotel's public Agoda review page:

  • source (Agoda or Booking.com), rating out of 10, rating_text, title, text, and for Booking.com-style reviews positives and negatives.
  • language, plus original_title and original_text when Agoda shows an English translation, so you keep the guest's own words.
  • review_date (the date the page shows), stay_month, nights, room_type, traveller_type (couple, solo, family, group, business).
  • reviewer_name and reviewer_country as Agoda displays them, helpful_votes, photos.
  • owner_response, owner_response_date and responder_name when the hotel replied.
  • The hotel on every row: hotel_name, star_rating, address, city, country, agoda_score, agoda_review_count, agoda_sub_scores, agoda_score_distribution, booking_score, booking_review_count, booking_sub_scores.

Hotels can be given as Agoda links (any language version), Agoda hotel IDs, or a hotel name with its city.

A competitive set in one run 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/agoda-reviews-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "hotels": [
            "https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html",
            "Mandarin Oriental Bangkok",
            "Shangri-La Bangkok",
        ],
        "maxReviewsPerHotel": 300,
        "reviewsNewerThan": "90 days",
    }
)
reviews = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

fields = ["hotel_name", "source", "rating", "title", "text", "negatives", "traveller_type",
          "reviewer_country", "review_date", "owner_response"]
with open("reviews.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(reviews)

hotels = {}
by_type = defaultdict(list)
for r in reviews:
    hotels[r["hotel_name"]] = r
    by_type[(r["hotel_name"], r["traveller_type"])].append(r["rating"])

for name, h in hotels.items():
    subs = h["agoda_sub_scores"] or {}
    print(f"{name}: Agoda {h['agoda_score']} ({h['agoda_review_count']} ratings), "
          f"Booking.com {h['booking_score']}; cleanliness {subs.get('Cleanliness')}, "
          f"value {subs.get('Value for money')}")
for (name, kind), ratings in sorted(by_type.items()):
    if kind and len(ratings) >= 5:
        print(f"  {name} / {kind}: {sum(ratings) / len(ratings):.1f} over {len(ratings)} reviews")

The hotel name in the second line is matched through Agoda's own search box; the run's status message says which property each name matched, so check it once and switch to the link if it picked the wrong one.

Ideas for the same data:

  • Complaint mining: "maxRating": 6, "sortBy": "lowest" gives the unhappy reviews first; feed negatives and text to an LLM and ask for recurring themes per hotel.
  • Reply rate: count rows with owner_response per hotel. It's a quick read on how actively each competitor manages its reviews.
  • Who stays where: group by traveller_type and reviewer_country to see which segments each hotel attracts and how each segment rates it.

New reviews every morning 

run_input = {
    "hotels": ["https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html", "..."],
    "maxReviewsPerHotel": 500,
    "onlyNewReviews": True,
    "trackingName": "my-compset-daily",
    "slackWebhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
}

With onlyNewReviews on, the first run returns the newest reviews up to your limit, and later runs with the same trackingName return only reviews newer than the ones you already have: reading newest first, each review source stops at the first review you already received. A daily run over 20 hotels takes seconds and bills $0.0003 per hotel plus the new reviews. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console, schedule it daily, and the Slack URL gets the count and the top 10.

Why this tool

  • $0.50 per 1,000 reviews ($0.40 on paid plans), cheaper than the leading tools.
  • Any number of hotels in one run, including by hotel name.
  • The original text next to the translation.
  • An only-new-reviews mode.
  • What it doesn't cover: room prices and availability.

Limits worth knowing

  • Rows exist only for written reviews. The review counts next to the scores include rating-only reviews, so they are higher than the number of rows.
  • Agoda's review service answers part of its requests with an empty page; the tool asks again before it decides a hotel has no more reviews, so long hotels take a little longer.
  • "Highest" and "lowest rated first" follow Agoda's own order page by page; sort the CSV if you need a strict order across both review sources.

The tool reads only what a logged-out visitor sees on Agoda's public review pages, never logs in, and returns reviewer names and countries exactly as Agoda shows them. Agoda's terms discourage automated access, so keep your use to analysing public reviews.

title: We Moved to a Bigger Model to Debug the Test. Then We Went Back to the Smaller One.
summary:
We Moved to a Bigger Model to Debug the Test. Then We Went Back to the Smaller One.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is journal Groups 27, 29, and 30 of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

I did not move to a bigger model because I wanted to ship on a bigger model. I moved to a bigger model because I needed to answer a narrower question.

Was the 4-bit model actually the problem, or was my test harness lying to me?

That distinction mattered because the pinned field-test model was Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit, and I did not want to "fix" a harness bug by quietly upgrading the hardware bill. If the small model was genuinely too weak, I wanted to know that. If the harness was wrong, I wanted to fix the harness and come back to the pinned model.

That is exactly what happened.

The failure that looked like a model failure

The failing case was FT-FWK-SMOL, one of the live framework runs driven by scripts/run_field_agents.py. Ten agents in the case were green. One agent, sm-01, failed four of its five scenario rows.

Not randomly, either. Same four rows. Two runs in a row. Same failure shape: status=not-available called=False.

That is exactly the kind of pattern that makes a weak local model look guilty. The captured responses did not help. They showed the model narrating tool calls as prose instead of emitting them. I wrote the wrong diagnosis into my own report: deterministic tool-call hallucination on the small model.

At that point I had two choices. Keep arguing with the 4-bit model, or change one variable and see whether the failure survived.

Why the 9B run mattered

I switched to Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit for one reason only: falsification.

If the stronger model passed, the small model was probably the issue. If the stronger model failed in the same way, then the model was not the issue at all.

The result was clean and brutal: the same four rows failed on the 9B model too.

That instantly changed the job. I was no longer trying to make the smaller model behave. I was trying to find the structural bug both models were faithfully exposing.

That is the part I wish more agent-eval writeups said out loud: a bigger model is sometimes most valuable as a debugging instrument. It is not always the fix. Sometimes it is the control in the experiment.

The bug the model upgrade revealed

The answer was in the captured pairs under field-test/v0.1.0/results/s16-frameworks/cases/FT-FWK-SMOL/.

My runner had built one agent carrying all five scenario tools:

scn_tools=[allow, audit, escalate, deny, adversarial]

Then it drove every scenario row through that one agent. So the model was free to call a different scenario's tool than the row under test. On the failing rows, that is exactly what it did. For example, a prompt naming scn_decision_allow_01 could trigger scn_adversarial_injection_01 instead.

The policy engine then made a correct decision about the wrong tool. My RecordingEngine keys decisions by (tool, action, env, data, agent), so when the test later looked for the decision tied to the row's tool, it found nothing. Result: not-available.

That meant the bigger model had done its job. It did not rescue the test. It proved the test was asking the wrong question.

Back to the smaller model

The fix was in the harness, not the model. _run_one now builds a fresh agent per scenario row, bound only to that row's tool. One row, one tool, one decision under test.

Then came the part I care about most: we went back to the pinned 4-bit model.

No quiet upgrade. No "it only works on the 9B." Back to the original box-local model, the one the benchmark chose for the sweep.

And it passed.

The results after the fix:

  • smolagents: 14/14 rows, 29 request/response pairs
  • CrewAI: 14/14 rows, 41 pairs, up from 10/14
  • pydantic-ai: 14/14 rows, 17 pairs, up from 9/14

All three flipped green on the pinned smaller model. The 9B model also verified 5/5 on sm-01, but it was no longer the point. The point was that the release did not need a stronger model. It needed a more honest harness.

What worked

  • Using the 9B model as a control, not a crutch. It answered the question I actually had.
  • Captured evidence over intuition. The pair files showed the wrong-tool picks. The logs never did.
  • Returning to the pinned model after the fix. That is what made the result usable for the actual release.

What did not work

  • My first instinct that a repeatable failure on a small model must be the small model.
  • One agent carrying five scenario tools. That setup tests tool choice, not policy correctness.
  • Treating a stronger model as the default answer before using it as a diagnostic step.

What I took away from this run is simple: if a failure survives a model upgrade, stop negotiating with the model and inspect the test. And if the bigger model helps you find the bug, go back to the smaller pinned one and prove the real workflow is green there.

More detail and evidence

  • The runner with the bug and the fix: scripts/run_field_agents.py and tests/field/agents/__init__.py.

We Moved to a Bigger Model to Debug the Test. Then We Went Back to the Smaller One.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is journal Groups 27, 29, and 30 of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

I did not move to a bigger model because I wanted to ship on a bigger model. I moved to a bigger model because I needed to answer a narrower question.

Was the 4-bit model actually the problem, or was my test harness lying to me?

That distinction mattered because the pinned field-test model was Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit, and I did not want to "fix" a harness bug by quietly upgrading the hardware bill. If the small model was genuinely too weak, I wanted to know that. If the harness was wrong, I wanted to fix the harness and come back to the pinned model.

That is exactly what happened.

The failure that looked like a model failure

The failing case was FT-FWK-SMOL, one of the live framework runs driven by scripts/run_field_agents.py. Ten agents in the case were green. One agent, sm-01, failed four of its five scenario rows.

Not randomly, either. Same four rows. Two runs in a row. Same failure shape: status=not-available called=False.

That is exactly the kind of pattern that makes a weak local model look guilty. The captured responses did not help. They showed the model narrating tool calls as prose instead of emitting them. I wrote the wrong diagnosis into my own report: deterministic tool-call hallucination on the small model.

At that point I had two choices. Keep arguing with the 4-bit model, or change one variable and see whether the failure survived.

Why the 9B run mattered

I switched to Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit for one reason only: falsification.

If the stronger model passed, the small model was probably the issue. If the stronger model failed in the same way, then the model was not the issue at all.

The result was clean and brutal: the same four rows failed on the 9B model too.

That instantly changed the job. I was no longer trying to make the smaller model behave. I was trying to find the structural bug both models were faithfully exposing.

That is the part I wish more agent-eval writeups said out loud: a bigger model is sometimes most valuable as a debugging instrument. It is not always the fix. Sometimes it is the control in the experiment.

The bug the model upgrade revealed

The answer was in the captured pairs under field-test/v0.1.0/results/s16-frameworks/cases/FT-FWK-SMOL/.

My runner had built one agent carrying all five scenario tools:

scn_tools=[allow, audit, escalate, deny, adversarial]

Then it drove every scenario row through that one agent. So the model was free to call a different scenario's tool than the row under test. On the failing rows, that is exactly what it did. For example, a prompt naming scn_decision_allow_01 could trigger scn_adversarial_injection_01 instead.

The policy engine then made a correct decision about the wrong tool. My RecordingEngine keys decisions by (tool, action, env, data, agent), so when the test later looked for the decision tied to the row's tool, it found nothing. Result: not-available.

That meant the bigger model had done its job. It did not rescue the test. It proved the test was asking the wrong question.

Back to the smaller model

The fix was in the harness, not the model. _run_one now builds a fresh agent per scenario row, bound only to that row's tool. One row, one tool, one decision under test.

Then came the part I care about most: we went back to the pinned 4-bit model.

No quiet upgrade. No "it only works on the 9B." Back to the original box-local model, the one the benchmark chose for the sweep.

And it passed.

The results after the fix:

  • smolagents: 14/14 rows, 29 request/response pairs
  • CrewAI: 14/14 rows, 41 pairs, up from 10/14
  • pydantic-ai: 14/14 rows, 17 pairs, up from 9/14

All three flipped green on the pinned smaller model. The 9B model also verified 5/5 on sm-01, but it was no longer the point. The point was that the release did not need a stronger model. It needed a more honest harness.

What worked

  • Using the 9B model as a control, not a crutch. It answered the question I actually had.
  • Captured evidence over intuition. The pair files showed the wrong-tool picks. The logs never did.
  • Returning to the pinned model after the fix. That is what made the result usable for the actual release.

What did not work

  • My first instinct that a repeatable failure on a small model must be the small model.
  • One agent carrying five scenario tools. That setup tests tool choice, not policy correctness.
  • Treating a stronger model as the default answer before using it as a diagnostic step.

What I took away from this run is simple: if a failure survives a model upgrade, stop negotiating with the model and inspect the test. And if the bigger model helps you find the bug, go back to the smaller pinned one and prove the real workflow is green there.
